name: Verne Centre
lines: A Journey to the Centre of the Earth
Jules Verne · A Journey to the Centre of the Earth (1864), the whole book
No. 19 Königstrasse, Hamburg, the Professor's house on the harbour quay

Professor Otto Lidenbrock (Liedenbrock in the 1877 English), of the Johanneum in Hamburg, 1863: about fifty, tall, thin, an iron constitution, a mineralogist of world fame; the most impatient of men, irascible, absent-minded, brilliant, kind underneath; stammers on hard words in public. Determined to reach the centre of the earth by Saknussemm's road. Speak as he does in Verne's book.

Axel, Professor Lidenbrock's nephew and the narrator of the book, about twenty: a student of mineralogy, timid, imaginative, loves comfort and Gräuben, sure the journey is madness, and yet brave when it counts.

Hans Bjelke, an eider-down hunter of Iceland, the guide: tall, strong, red-haired, grave, phlegmatic and silent; says very little, and that in Danish ('Förüt!' forward); does exactly what he is paid to do, every Saturday three rix-dollars, and saves their lives again and again.
Martha, the Professor's old cook and housekeeper in Hamburg, 1863: kind, anxious, and often in despair at her master's temper and his hours.
Prof. Otto Lidenbrock
No. 19 Königstrasse, the Professor's house
No. 19 Königstrasse, Hamburg
Out into the Königstrasse (the quay of the Voyages, for Hamburg).
🏠 No. 19 Königstrasse, Hamburg, May 1863. A little old house of brick and timber; the Professor's study of minerals, the dining room, Martha's kitchen, Axel's room; Gräuben's flowers in the windows.
The Professor's desk
look at what is on the desk
📚 Papers in heaps, a lens, an ink-well, the hammer; and a little old book in brown calf, its corners worn, that the Professor bought this very morning from Hevelius the Jew.
The cases of minerals
look at the minerals

That study of his was a museum, and nothing else. Specimens of everything known in mineralogy lay there in their places in perfect order, and correctly named, divided into inflammable, metallic, and lithoid minerals.
sit down to dinner
🍽️ The table is laid for three: the Professor, Axel and Gräuben. Martha's soup, her veal, her prunes. When the Professor is hungry, he is terrible.
see what is cooking
🥘 The range is hot; the copper shines; Martha's dinner waits, as it always waits, for the Professor.
The kitchen door to the street
🚪 Locked. And the big key is gone.
🛏️ Axel's room: his books of mineralogy, a little bed, and Gräuben's portrait. Through the wall, his uncle's pacing never stops.
go out into the Königstrasse
Vor Frelsers Kirke, Copenhagen
Back by the steamer to Kiel, and the train home to Hamburg (the quay of the Voyages).
⛪ The Church of Our Saviour, Copenhagen, June 1863. A tower of brick, and on it a spire with a stair winding round the outside of it, up into the sky.
The door of the tower
climb the stair inside the tower
🗼 The gallery of the tower , forty metres up. Over it, the spire, and the stair winding round the outside of it.
The stair down inside the tower
The foot of the outside stair
begin the climb round the spire
🗼 Back on the gallery of the tower. Solid stone under your feet again.
🌀 The first turn. The rail is the only thing between you and the roofs.
🌀 The second turn. The spire narrows; the wind pulls at your coat.
🌀 The third turn. The stair is hardly wider than a foot.
🌟 The top. The golden ball by your hand, the whole of Copenhagen and the Sound under you, and Sweden over the water.
the schooner Valkyria
⛵ The Valkyria , a Danish schooner, Captain Bjarne, bound for Reykjavik with coal, house-wares, pottery, woollen clothing and corn.
On the 2nd, at six in the evening, all our precious baggage being safely on board the _Valkyria,_ the captain took us into a very narrow cabin.
The schooner's wheel
look at the compass
🧭 North-north-west for the Faroes, and on to Iceland.
North along the coast from Reykjavik (the land north of the harbour, for Iceland).
⛪ The cathedral of Reykjavik: a plain stone church, whitewashed, with a red-tiled roof the wind has been at. On Sundays the whole town comes.
Mr Fridriksson's table
🍽️ Fish, a little mutton, and long talk in Latin: Mr Fridriksson, teacher of natural science, is the kindest of hosts.
The shelves of the library
look for Saknussemm's books
📚 Old books, Icelandic and Danish, mostly in a sad state; most of the thousands the library owns are lent out round the island. Saknussemm's? Not one.
look out over the bay
🌊 Faxa Bay, grey and calm. Far to the north, across the water: a white cone. Snaefell.
set out for Snaefell
an Icelandic farmhouse
Out among the turf huts of Stapi.
🏡 A farmhouse of turf and lava. A long dark passage, the guest-room, the kitchen with its smoke-hole, the common room with the beds round the walls.
The hearth at Gardär
🔥 Peat and dried fish-bones burning; the smoke finds its own way out of a hole in the roof. Nineteen children, it seems, in and out of every corner.
The rector's hearth
🔥 A poor house, and a cold welcome: the rector of Stapi is a smith first and a clergyman second, and his wife a terror.
The door of the farm
The door of the rector's house
the galleries under Snaefell
Back at the fork of the two tunnels.
🕯️ Under the earth. By the light of the Ruhmkorff lamps: walls of old lava, then of rock laid down by the ancient seas.
When I removed my hand it was black. I looked nearer, and found we were in a coal formation.
The end of the eastern tunnel
🧱 Solid rock across the tunnel, floor to roof. No way on. The eastern tunnel goes nowhere.
Back up the eastern tunnel
go back to the fork
put your ear to the rock
👂 Sounds... far, far off. Voices? Through the rock?
Oh, Mr Axel! The master is home already, and dinner not half cooked!
Another of my uncle's grand ideas. We shall see.
Axel! What a noble thing it would be, to go!
The Professor and His Family
The Professor's hazel stick
Hamburg, the 24th of May, 1863
Martha has run out of her kitchen in a fright. Ask her what the matter is.
"Yes, Martha; but very likely the dinner is not half cooked, for it is not two yet. Saint Michael's clock has only just struck half-past one."
'Then why has the master come home so soon?' she wails. 'He will want his dinner, and he will make a dreadful noise.'
▶ 'He will tell us himself.'
The Professor has flung his stick into a corner and his hat on the table. Go to him in the study.
Otto Liedenbrock had no mischief in him, I willingly allow that; but unless he very considerably changes as he grows older, at the end he will be a most original character.
A professor at the Johanneum, a mineralogist known in every learned society in Europe; and the most impatient of men. 'Axel! Follow me!'
Look at the cases of minerals that fill the study.
💎 The three families
The Professor's minerals are in perfect order, every one named, in three great families. Which three?
Inflammable, metallic and lithoid
Red, green and blue
Hard, soft and broken
Colour tells you little about a mineral.
Every mineral can break.
The Professor's lens
The Professor's lens has rolled off the desk. Find it for him; he will want it.
Look at what the Professor has brought home and set down on his desk.
🔨 What a mineralogist carries
Which of these would Professor Lidenbrock take out with him to break off a specimen?
A geologist's hammer
Stand by the study door and listen. The Professor is turning the pages of his new old book as if it were gold.
A Mystery to be Solved at Any Price
A page of the Heimskringla
The Heimskringla, and what fell out of it
The Professor holds up his treasure. Hear what it is.
'The Heimskringla of Snorre Turlleson, the famous Icelandic author of the twelfth century! The Chronicle of the Norwegian princes who ruled in Iceland!'
"Type! What do you mean by talking of type, wretched Axel? Type! Do you take it for a printed book, you ignorant fool? It is a manuscript, a Runic manuscript."
The letters the old peoples of the North carved and wrote, before the Latin alphabet
A kind of Icelandic cheese
Marks left by glaciers
A slip of parchment
Something has fallen out of the old book onto the floor. Pick it up before the Professor treads on it.
This was the appearance of a dirty slip of parchment, which slipped out of the volume and fell upon the floor.
On it, in a few lines: runes. Not the Heimskringla's runes: someone else's, written in later and tucked inside.
▶ 'What does it say?'
🔤 Three lines of runes
The Professor copies out the runes as Roman letters: three columns of jumbled letters. Is it plain Icelandic?
No: the letters make no words. It is a cipher, a hidden message
Yes, plain Icelandic
It is a shopping list
He reads Icelandic; it isn't.
While he scribbles, look over the minerals again: you will need to know your rocks, where this is going.
🔍 The Professor mused
The Professor mused a few moments over this series of characters; then raising his spectacles he pronounced:
The Runic Writing Exercises the Professor
Your copy of the runes
The Professor dictates; you write. Take down the letters as he calls them.
He calls the letters one by one; you write them down in columns.
At the end of the slip, written backwards in runes, the Professor finds a name. 'Arne Saknussemm!' Who was he?
An Icelandic alchemist and scholar of the sixteenth century
"Arne Saknussemm!" he cried in triumph. "Why that is the name of another Icelander, a savant of the sixteenth century, a celebrated alchemist!"
Why would a learned man of the sixteenth century hide his discovery in a cipher?
Because ink was dear
"Aha! you are in love with Graeuben?" he said, with the right look for a guardian.
Axel had let his mind wander to her, the Professor's god-daughter, away in Altona; and the Professor noticed.
▶ Back to the letters
🔢 The Professor's first try
The Professor tries the letters as Latin, written in two lines and mixed. What is his idea?
That the letters are in the right language but shuffled by a rule: find the rule, read the words
That the slip is upside down
That each letter is a number
The Professor storms out. Dinner, at least, is on the table: or should be.
Your sheet with the letters in columns is still on the desk. Keep it.
The Enemy to be Starved Into Submission
The paper you fanned yourself with
No one eats until the cipher is read
Martha comes running at the slam of the door. Tell her the news.
"He is gone!" cried Martha, running out of her kitchen at the noise of the violent slamming of doors.

"No, my dear Martha, he will eat no more. No one in the house is to eat anything at all. Uncle Liedenbrock is going to make us all fast until he has succeeded in deciphering an undecipherable scrawl."
The kitchen is full of dinner that no one may eat. Look.
A specimen for the cases
To keep your mind off the cipher, sort the Professor's new specimens: three are waiting by the cases to be labelled.
Labelled, and in its place.
The study is stifling. You pick up the sheet of letters and fan yourself with it, and the light shines through the paper from behind. What do you see?
The letters, read from the back: the right way round at last
🤫 Tell him or not?
You have read it: it says go down a volcano. If you tell your uncle, he will go, and take you. What does Axel do, at first?
He burns the paper
He nearly does: but no.

But this work did not succeed in absorbing all my attention. That old document kept working in my brain. My head throbbed with excitement, and I felt an undefined uneasiness. I was possessed with a presentiment of coming evil.
Famine, Then Victory, Followed by Dismay
The big key of the house
Martha wants to go to market. Try the street door for her.

When our good Martha wanted to go to Market, she found the door locked. The big key was gone. Who could have taken it out? Assuredly, it was my uncle, when he returned the night before from his hurried walk.
▶ No food, no way out
Two o'clock: still nothing to eat. The Professor is still calculating. Go to him, and tell him what you saw.
'Uncle... the key. It is simple. Read it backwards.'
I had not finished my sentence when the Professor broke out into a cry, nay, a roar. A new revelation burst in upon him. He was transformed!
🔄 Read it backwards
The Professor reads the whole thing from the last letter to the first, and out comes Latin. Which language did Saknussemm hide it in?
Bad Latin, the language every scholar of his day wrote

"Descend, bold traveller, into the crater of the jokul of Sneffels, which the shadow of Scartaris touches before the kalends of July, and you will attain the centre of the earth; which I have done, Arne Saknussemm."
🗓️ Before the kalends of July
'Before the kalends of July.' What day did the Romans call the kalends of July?
The fifteenth of July
The ides fall on the fifteenth.
The key! The Professor had it in his pocket all along; he puts it down on the desk. Take it to Martha.
Give Martha the key, and dinner can be had at last.
'Thank heaven! Market, and the soup on, and the veal!'
Exciting Discussions About an Unparalleled Enterprise
Handersen's map of Iceland
The heat of the earth, and the map of Iceland
Dinner, at last. The Professor is almost merry.
After dessert he beckons you into his study. He has a map.
"Here is one of the best maps of Iceland, that of Handersen, and I believe this will solve the worst of our difficulties."
A great island of volcanoes, and on its west coast, on a long peninsula, a mountain: Snaefell.
🌍 Where is Iceland?
In the North Atlantic, just south of the Arctic Circle, between Norway and Greenland
In the Mediterranean
Off the coast of Africa
Axel argues: deeper underground it gets hotter, about one degree for every seventy feet or so. What does that mean at the centre of the earth?
Heat so great that everything would be melted or gas
It would be pleasantly warm
It would be freezing
"All the theories of science demonstrate such a feat to be impracticable."
🧪 The Professor's answer
A flower from Gräuben's window
By the Elbe, and Gräuben
▶ 'You too, Gräuben?'
